The desired visit includes receiving encouragement

Paul has wanted to visit Rome and has been prevented (verse 13). Verse 11 says he wants to give them a spiritual gift. Verse 12 corrects that at once with “that is.” He will be encouraged too, by their faith and his together. The gift runs both ways. Verse 15 keeps his aim plain: to tell the good news in Rome.
Judging others does not remove the judge from judgment

Chapter 1 ended with a list of wrongs that a reader could condemn. Verse 1 begins with “therefore” and turns on that reader. The one who judges does the same things. So the verdict he gives on others falls on himself. Verse 3 asks if he thinks he will escape. Verse 4 names what he has missed: God’s kindness was meant to bring repentance. Verse 11 gives the rule under all of it: God has no favorites.
One God prevents either people from owning the gift

Verse 27 asks where boasting is, and answers that it is shut out. Verse 28 says a person is justified by faith, apart from works of law. Verse 29 tests that with a question about God. If the law were the way, God would be the God of Jews only. Verse 30 answers that there is one God. He justifies the circumcised and the uncircumcised by the same faith. Verse 31 adds that this does not cancel the law.
Abraham's trust comes before the sign

Verse 9 asks whether the blessing is only for the circumcised. Verse 10 answers with the order of events in Abraham’s life. He was counted righteous first and circumcised later. Verse 11 then calls circumcision a sign and seal of the faith he already had. That order makes him father of two groups. He is father of all who believe without circumcision (verse 11). He is also father of the circumcised who walk in that faith (verse 12).
The gift arrives while its recipients remain enemies

Verse 5 says hope does not disappoint, because God’s love is poured out. Verses 6–8 show how that love is known. Verse 7 sets the human limit: one will hardly die even for a righteous person. Verse 8 puts Christ’s death outside that limit. He died for us “while we were yet sinners.” The timing is the proof. Verse 10 argues from it: enemies were reconciled, so the reconciled will be saved.
Baptism joins death with a changed way of living

Verse 1 raises an objection to chapter 5. If grace grows where sin grows, why not sin more? Verse 2 says those who died to sin cannot go on living in it. Verse 4 explains that death by what baptism does. The baptized are buried with Christ into his death. The purpose follows: as Christ was raised, they walk in new life. Verse 11 tells them to count themselves dead to sin and alive to God.
The law is good even when sin uses its command

Verse 5 said sinful passions worked “through the law.” That could sound as if the law itself is sin (verse 7). Paul separates the two. The law showed him what coveting is (verse 7). Sin took the command as its opening and deceived him (verses 8 and 11). Verse 12 therefore clears the law: it is holy, righteous, and good. Verse 13 places the blame: sin worked death through a good thing.
The Spirit helps within weakness rather than removing every groan

Verses 22–23 describe two groans: creation’s and the believers’. Both wait for something not yet seen (verses 24–25). Verse 26 adds a third groan, and it is the Spirit’s. The weakness it names is exact: we do not know how to pray. The Spirit pleads for us with groans that cannot be spoken. Verse 27 says God, who searches hearts, knows the Spirit’s mind.
The argument begins with grief and Israel's received gifts

Chapter 8 ended with nothing able to separate believers from God’s love. That raises a question about Israel, and Paul starts with grief (verse 2). He would accept being cut off for their sake (verse 3). Verse 4 then lists what is theirs, in the present tense. Adoption, glory, covenants, the law, the service, and the promises are theirs. Verse 5 adds the fathers and the Christ. Only after that does verse 6 say God’s word has not failed.
Calling depends on hearing, and hearing depends on sent speakers

Verse 13 promises that whoever calls on the Lord’s name will be saved. Verse 14 asks what must come before that call. The questions step backward: calling needs belief, belief needs hearing, hearing needs a speaker. Verse 15 adds the last step: the speaker must be sent. Verse 17 sums it up: faith comes by hearing. Then verse 18 asks if Israel has heard, and answers yes. Verse 21 ends with God’s hands held out all day to Israel.
The added branches must not boast against their supporting root

Verse 13 says Paul now speaks to Gentiles. Verse 17 gives their place: wild olive branches grafted in among the others. They share the root; they did not grow it. Verse 18 forbids boasting over the broken branches and gives the reason. The root holds them up, and they do not hold up the root. Verse 20 says they stand only by faith and should fear. Verse 23 adds that God can graft the others in again.
Peace requires effort without pretending one person controls every response

Verse 17 forbids paying back evil with evil. Verse 18 gives the positive side and adds two limits. “If it is possible” admits that peace may not be reached. “As much as it is up to you” marks the part a person controls. The other person’s answer is not in that part. Verse 19 names what is given up: revenge belongs to God. Verse 20 names what remains to do: give an enemy food and drink.
Love explains the commands through the harm they prevent

Verse 7 says to pay everyone what is owed. Verse 8 names one debt that stays open: love for one another. Verse 9 lists commands, and each forbids a harm to someone else. Verse 10 gives the reason love covers them. Love does no harm to a neighbor. So one who loves has done what those commands require.
Welcome refuses to turn disputed practices into judgment of another servant

Two groups disagree about food and days (verses 2 and 5). Verses 3–4 tell each to stop despising or judging the other. Verse 14 gives Paul’s own view: no food is unclean in itself. He does not use that view to settle the matter. Verse 15 says food must not destroy one for whom Christ died. Verse 19 states the aim that replaces winning: peace and building one another up. Verse 20 names the other course: tearing down God’s work for food.
Shared welcome extends into practical support and uncertain travel plans

Chapter 14 dealt with believers who judged each other over food and days. Verse 7 gives the rule that ends that section. They are to accept one another as Christ accepted them. Verses 8–9 show what that acceptance covered. Christ served the circumcised to confirm the promises to the fathers. He did it so that the Gentiles also might glorify God. Verse 26 shows it in practice: Gentile assemblies send money to Jerusalem’s poor.
The greetings make shared work and needed help visible

Phoebe is named first, before any greeting (verse 1). Paul calls her “our sister” and a servant of the assembly at Cenchreae. Verse 2 asks two things for her. The Romans should receive her in a way worthy of the saints. They should also help her in whatever she needs. The reason given is her record: she has helped many, and Paul himself. The request asks them to return what she has given.
